beats.narration: Investor day is in three weeks.
Cy has promised a Sprout Pro: a keypad to set schedules, a small display, a watering history stored in memory, and a light sensor so Sprout knows night from day.
Everything we have learned, all in one device. How hard can it be?
Each piece is easy. Putting them together is the hard part. Today is about systems: how parts fit, how data flows, and how fast it all needs to go.
First, the keypad. Twelve buttons: the digits, a star, and a hash. Wiring each to its own pin would use twelve pins. The trick is a key matrix.
The buttons sit at the crossings of four row wires and three column wires. Seven pins instead of twelve. A sixteen key pad needs eight pins instead of sixteen.
To read it, the code drives one row low at a time and reads the columns.
If a column reads low while row two is driven, the key at row two, that column, is pressed. Scanning all rows takes a fraction of a millisecond.
What if someone presses three keys at once?
With some combinations, a phantom fourth key appears, because current sneaks through the pressed switches. Diodes on each key prevent that ghosting.
For a schedule keypad, we will simply ignore multiple presses.
Each key still bounces, so the matrix scan runs from a timer every few milliseconds, with the same debounce logic as before, just for twelve keys at once.
Keypads also need a little user interface thinking. What happens if someone holds a key? Auto-repeat after half a second. What if they press nothing for a minute?
Time out and return to the home screen.
And a beep. Every key should beep.
Every key will beep. The office will hate us.
Small details like these turn a technically working keypad into one that feels good. They are part of the system too, and they need time in the schedule.
Next, the display. There are many kinds: single LEDs, seven-segment digits, character screens, and pixel displays.
A pixel display, even a small one, holds a lot of data.
A one hundred twenty-eight by sixty-four monochrome screen is eight thousand one hundred ninety-two pixels, a kilobyte of memory just for one frame.
The code keeps a frame buffer in RAM, draws text and icons into it, and sends it to the display over SPI.
Only changed areas need to be resent, which saves time.
Fonts eat flash. Every character of every size is a little bitmap. Choose one or two fonts, not twelve.
There is a subtle problem with updating a display.
If we redraw the frame buffer while it is being sent to the screen, the top half shows the old picture and the bottom half the new one.
That glitch is called tearing.
The fix is the same idea as with DMA: two buffers. Draw into one while the other is being sent, then swap.
It doubles the memory cost, so on a tiny chip, you might instead only redraw areas that are not being sent.
Or use a display with its own memory, which keeps the picture even when the chip stops sending.
Then we only send changes, and the chip can sleep while the screen keeps showing the moisture level.
Ada designs the screens: a moisture bar, a water drop icon, a clock. Many elements repeat. The same drop icon appears on four different screens.
If each screen stored its own copy of every icon, we would run out of memory. Instead, we store each icon once, in flash, and screens just point to it.
That is the flyweight pattern: share the heavy, unchanging part, keep only the small varying part separate.
Each screen keeps only where to draw the icon. The pixels live in one place. With dozens of icons and characters, the savings are enormous.
And to create those screen elements, we use a factory: a single function that takes a description, like a button with this label at this position, and builds the right object.
The rest of the code never deals with construction details.
So if we change how icons are built, only the factory changes. Every screen keeps calling ui make.

beats.narration: Sprout Pro must remember its settings and watering history when the batteries are swapped. RAM forgets everything without power. So the data goes into flash memory.
Flash has strange rules. You cannot simply overwrite a byte. Writing can only change ones to zeros.

beats.narration: For settings, a key-value store is even friendlier. Save a value under a name, like water amount, and read it back by name.
Internally, it appends records and keeps the latest one for each key.
For larger data, like a long watering history, a small file system designed for flash handles wear leveling, and crucially, survives power loss in the middle of a write without corrupting everything.
Power loss is the real test. Pull the batteries mid-save, a hundred times. If the data comes back sane every time, you have a storage design you can trust.
Now the light sensor. Ben has two options: an analog light sensor that outputs a voltage, and a digital one that speaks I squared C.
Analog sensors are simple and cheap, but the code must convert voltages into meaningful units, and calibrate for each sensor's quirks.
Electrical noise on the wire becomes noise in your data.
Digital sensors do the conversion internally and send calibrated numbers. Many add features: configurable ranges, alerts, low power modes. The cost is a driver, and reading a longer datasheet.
We go digital for light. But the soil probe stays analog, because there are no cheap digital soil sensors that survive being buried in mud.
Ada wants different watering behavior for different plants. A cactus wants rare, deep watering. A fern wants frequent, gentle sips. Same inputs, different decisions.
Instead of an enormous if statement, we use the strategy pattern: each watering style is a separate, swappable algorithm with the same interface.
The watering logic calls the current strategy's dose function. Choosing cactus mode just switches a pointer. New plant types do not touch the core logic.
We can sell plant packs! Orchid mode, three ninety-nine!
And there it is.
Sensor data rarely arrives ready to use. It needs cleaning, converting, and combining.
A clean way to organize that is a pipeline: a chain of small stages, each doing one job.
Each stage takes data in, transforms it, and passes it on. Remove spikes throws out readings that are wildly different from their neighbors. Average smooths the noise. Convert applies calibration.
Decide uses the result.
Because stages share a simple interface, you can test each one alone, reorder them, or insert a new one, like temperature compensation, without rewriting the others.
And it matches how engineers think about signals. You can draw it on a whiteboard, and the code looks just like the drawing.
Finally, the question that ties a system together: is it fast enough, and is there room?
Engineers sometimes call this speeds and feeds: how much data flows through each part, and how fast each part can handle it.
For each path, compare the rate you need with the rate available, and leave a healthy margin.
Sending one kilobyte to the display five times a second over an eight megabit SPI bus takes about five milliseconds per second. That is fine.
The danger is in the combinations.
The display update, the sensor read, and a flash write can all want the same bus, or the same processor time, at the same moment.
So, those two spikes?
Flash writes landing on top of display refreshes. The average load is low, but the peaks are what break deadlines. We stagger them so they never coincide.
That is the heart of system design: knowing the worst case, not just the average. Measure peak loads, not just totals.
Memory gets the same treatment. We add up every buffer: the display frame, the ring buffers, the stacks, the history cache.
Then we compare against the eight kilobytes the chip has.
Roughly forty percent free. That margin is not waste. It is the space where next year's features will live, and the cushion that keeps a surprise from becoming a crash.
Can we use the free part for the plant music?
No.
To recap. A key matrix reads many buttons with few pins. Displays need memory for frames and fonts, and flyweights keep shared images from multiplying.

beats.narration: Flash memory wears out, so wear leveling, key-value stores, and power-safe file systems protect your data. Analog sensors trade simplicity for calibration work; digital ones trade price for convenience.
